title: Choosing a database and indexing it
summary: SQL or NoSQL by access pattern, not by hype. B-tree indexes, composite column order, covering indexes and the write cost of each one, and reading EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to find the sequential scan.

steps.title: Start from the queries
body: "SQL or NoSQL?" is the wrong first question. Write down the **access patterns** first: which queries, how
often, by which key, with what consistency. Then pick the store that serves them.
| Store | Good at | Pay for it with |
| Relational (PostgreSQL, MySQL) | transactions across rows, constraints, joins, ad-hoc queries | one primary for writes; scaling writes past one machine needs sharding |

| Key-value / wide-column (DynamoDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB) | huge write rates and data sizes when every read knows its partition key | queries you did not design for are slow or impossible; joins are your job |
| Document (MongoDB, PostgreSQL `jsonb`) | reading and writing a whole aggregate (an order with its lines) | cross-document constraints and reporting |
| Search index (OpenSearch, Elasticsearch) | full text, relevance, facets | not a source of truth: rebuilt from the database |
A common default for a new service is PostgreSQL: it does relational work well, stores JSON, and one
large machine goes a long way. Move a workload elsewhere when a **requirement** forces it (write rate,
data size, latency at a key), not because the other store is fashionable.

steps.prompt: Which store fits each workload best?
items: Orders and payments that must commit together, plus monthly finance reports
Ad-hoc questions from analysts joining customers, orders and refunds
Session lookups by session id at 200,000 reads/s
2 million sensor readings a second, always read by device and time range
Product search with typo tolerance and facets
"Find tickets mentioning *refund* and *late*" ranked by relevance

steps.title: Indexes: what they buy and what they cost
body: A **B-tree index** keeps a column's values sorted with pointers to the rows, so finding one value is a
few page reads instead of a scan of the whole table.
- **Composite index**: an index on several columns, sorted by the first, then the second. It serves
queries on a **leftmost prefix**: `(customer_id, created_at)` helps `WHERE customer_id = 7` and
`WHERE customer_id = 7 AND created_at > ...`, but not `WHERE created_at > ...` alone.
- Put **equality** columns first and the **range** (or sort) column last. After a range condition, later
columns cannot narrow the search.
- **Covering index**: holds every column the query needs (`INCLUDE (total)` in PostgreSQL), so the plan
is an Index Only Scan and never touches the table.
- **Selectivity**: an index on `status` with three values rarely helps; the planner prefers a scan when a
condition matches a large share of rows.
Every index costs on **every write**: one more B-tree to update, more WAL, more memory to keep hot.
Ten indexes on a hot table can make inserts several times slower. Index for the queries you run, check
`pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan` for indexes nobody uses, and drop them.

steps.prompt: The busiest query on the orders page is below. Which index serves it best?
code: WHERE customer_id = $1 AND created_at > now() - interval '30 days'
options: Two separate indexes on `customer_id` and on `created_at`
steps.explain: Equality first, range last: the index jumps to this customer, then reads their last 30 days already sorted by `created_at`, and stops after 20 rows. Starting with `created_at` scans everyone's last 30 days. Add `INCLUDE (total)` to make it covering.

steps.title: Reading the plan
body: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` runs the query and shows what the planner chose, with real row counts,
times and pages read. Read it from the most indented line outwards:
```text
Limit  (actual time=2131.4..2131.5 rows=20 loops=1)
->  Sort  (actual time=2131.4..2131.4 rows=20 loops=1)
Sort Key: created_at DESC
->  Seq Scan on orders  (actual time=0.03..2129.8 rows=41 loops=1)
Filter: ((customer_id = 7) AND (created_at > ...))
Rows Removed by Filter: 11999959
Buffers: shared hit=2210 read=148790
Execution Time: 2131.9 ms
- **Seq Scan** with a huge **Rows Removed by Filter**: it read 12 million rows to keep 41. A missing index.
- **Buffers: read=148790**: 148,790 pages (8 KB each, about 1.2 GB) came from disk or the OS cache, not
from PostgreSQL's shared buffers.
- Compare **estimated** rows (plain `EXPLAIN`) with **actual** rows: a big gap means stale statistics
(`ANALYZE orders;`).

prompt: **Symptom first.** After a feature launch, p99 for `GET /orders` went from 30 ms to 2.2 s and database CPU
is at 100 %. App CPU is 25 %. The plan above is for the new query. What do you do?
options: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on `orders (customer_id, created_at)`, then confirm the new plan with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
Move the database to a machine with twice the CPUs
Add a cache in front of the query and leave the plan alone
steps.explain: A bigger machine halves a 2-second scan at best; an index makes it a few milliseconds. `CONCURRENTLY` builds the index without blocking writes (it takes longer and cannot run inside a transaction). A cache hides the problem until the first miss storm.

steps.prompt: Match each plan node to what it tells you.
pairs: Every row of the table was read
The index found the rows, then the table was read for their columns
The index alone had every column needed
Matching row locations were collected from an index, then the table pages read in order
The sort did not fit in `work_mem` and spilled to disk

steps.prompt: Add the index for the orders page without blocking writes on a busy table.
steps.explain: `ONLINE` is SQL Server and Oracle syntax; PostgreSQL says `CONCURRENTLY`. If a concurrent build fails it leaves an INVALID index behind: drop it and try again.

steps.title: Which index can the query use?
prompt: - `int UsefulPrefix(string[] indexColumns, string[] equalityColumns, string? rangeColumn)`: walk the index
columns in order. Count each column that is in `equalityColumns`. The first column that is not: if it is
`rangeColumn`, count it too; either way, stop there.
- `string? BestIndex(Dictionary<string, string[]> indexes, string[] equalityColumns, string? rangeColumn)`:
the index name with the largest useful prefix (`0` means unusable). Ties go to the index with **fewer**
columns, then to the name in ordinal order. Return `null` if no index is usable.
`(customer_id, created_at)` with `customer_id = ...` and a range on `created_at` gives `2`;
starter: int UsefulPrefix(string[] indexColumns, string[] equalityColumns, string? rangeColumn)
string? BestIndex(Dictionary<string, string[]> indexes, string[] equalityColumns, string? rangeColumn)
solution: int UsefulPrefix(string[] indexColumns, string[] equalityColumns, string? rangeColumn)
string? BestIndex(Dictionary<string, string[]> indexes, string[] equalityColumns, string? rangeColumn)
.Select(kv => (Name: kv.Key, Columns: kv.Value.Length, Prefix: UsefulPrefix(kv.Value, equalityColumns, rangeColumn)))
hints: In `UsefulPrefix`, `continue` after an equality column; `break` at the first column that is not one (after counting it if it is the range column).
For `BestIndex`, compute the prefix of every index, drop the zeros, and sort: prefix descending, column count ascending, name ordinal.
template: Dojo.Eq("equality then range: both columns", 2, UsefulPrefix(new[] { "customer_id", "created_at" }, dojoEq, "created_at"));
Dojo.Eq("range first: it stops after the range", 1, UsefulPrefix(new[] { "created_at", "customer_id" }, dojoEq, "created_at"));
Dojo.Eq("an unrelated leading column: unusable", 0, UsefulPrefix(new[] { "status" }, dojoEq, "created_at"));
Dojo.Eq("a gap in the middle stops the prefix", 1, UsefulPrefix(new[] { "customer_id", "status", "created_at" }, dojoEq, "created_at"));
Dojo.Eq("no gap with status filtered too", 3, UsefulPrefix(new[] { "customer_id", "status", "created_at" }, new[] { "customer_id", "status" }, "created_at"));
Dojo.Eq("a second column alone is not a prefix", 0, UsefulPrefix(new[] { "a", "b" }, new[] { "b" }, null));
Dojo.Eq("the orders page picks the composite index", "orders_customer_created", BestIndex(dojoIdx, dojoEq, "created_at"));
Dojo.Eq("a lookup by id picks the primary key", "orders_pkey", BestIndex(dojoIdx, new[] { "id" }, null));
Dojo.Eq("a filter on an unindexed column: no index", (string?)null, BestIndex(dojoIdx, new[] { "total" }, null));
var dojoTie = new Dictionary<string, string[]> { ["a_wide"] = new[] { "customer_id", "note" }, ["b_narrow"] = new[] { "customer_id" } };
Dojo.Eq("a tie goes to the narrower index", "b_narrow", BestIndex(dojoTie, dojoEq, null));
steps.explain: Real planners also weigh selectivity, sort order and cost estimates, but the leftmost-prefix rule explains most "why is my index not used?" questions in review.

steps.title: Build it: the slow query
prompt: In the **System design board**, open *The slow query*. p99 is measured in seconds and the database is at
100 % while the app servers are idle. The budget does not allow a much bigger database. Find the cause in
the database settings and fix it, then run the load test until the goals are met.
steps.explain: A missing index multiplies the work of every query. No amount of hardware is as cheap as the index.
